The headline attribution is that the 16th Centre directs several threat groups, including Turla, an espionage crew that researchers have tracked for more than a decade under names like Snake and Uroburos. The EU's account covers both spying and sabotage: cyber operations against strategic French government entities going back to 2010 and its defense industry in 2025, and, in Poland, disruptive sabotage against critical infrastructure that included combined heat and power plants. France, Germany, Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Finland all appear on the target list, along with Ukraine.

Now the honest part. Sanctions on FSB officers aren't going to freeze anyone's holiday plans in Nice. These people weren't banking in Frankfurt. The mechanism's real product isn't financial pain, it's attribution: a government putting its name behind the claim that one identifiable Russian unit ran a decade of operations, and two governments doing it in lockstep rather than issuing separate statements a month apart.

For a SOC, the useful part is the mapping. When states formally tie the 16th Centre to Turla and to named sabotage campaigns, threat intelligence gets a firmer backbone. The activity you're modeling has an org chart now, not just a cluster of overlapping indicators. Whether naming it changes what Moscow does is a separate question, and the track record says attribution rarely slows these groups down. It does make them easier to talk about, and easier to hunt.

item.title: CISA Flags an Exploited Oracle E-Business Suite Payments Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-46817, an unauthenticated flaw that can hand attackers control of Oracle Payments, to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog with a July 18 federal fix deadline.
item.content:encoded:
An unauthenticated attacker who can reach your Oracle E-Business Suite over HTTP may be able to take over its payments module. No login required. CISA thinks someone already is.

On July 15 the agency added CVE-2026-46817 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The flaw sits in Oracle Payments, part of E-Business Suite, and it's really a stack of authentication failures bundled together: improper privilege management, improper authentication, and missing authentication for a critical function. The plain-language version is that the checks meant to confirm who you are and what you're allowed to do aren't reliably there.

Federal civilian agencies have until July 18 to patch it. That's three days from the listing. CISA's usual remediation window runs longer, and this time the agency didn't publish indicators of compromise or name a threat actor. When CISA sets a short fuse and stays quiet on the details, the message tends to be the same: this is being used in the wild, and explaining how would help the wrong people more than the defenders.

Oracle's E-Business Suite has been a rewarding target before. Late last year the Cl0p ransomware crew tore through EBS zero-days to steal data from dozens of organizations. Payments is exactly the module an attacker would want if the goal is fraud or extortion, because it sits on top of financial records, payment workflows, and whatever downstream enterprise systems the platform is wired into.

If you run E-Business Suite, treat this as tonight's work, not next sprint's. Apply Oracle's fix and then pull access logs for the payments endpoints, going back further than feels necessary, because a spot on the KEV list means exploitation predates the public disclosure. Worth noting: CISA added an older KNX building-automation flaw, CVE-2023-4346, the same day. Known-exploited and newly-discovered are not the same thing, and attackers are happy to use whichever one you forgot to patch.

item.title: ASML Raises Its 2026 Forecast Again as AI Chip Orders Pile Up
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: ASML posted 9.3 billion euros in Q2 sales and lifted its full-year outlook to 43-45 billion euros, crediting extremely strong orders for AI chip gear.
item.content:encoded:
9.3 billion euros in sales and a raised outlook, for the second time this year. That's ASML's second quarter, and for anyone trying to work out whether the AI buildout is real demand or a good story, it's about as close to ground truth as the chip industry offers.

The company reported 9.3 billion euros in net sales and 2.9 billion in net income, both ahead of expectations. It then raised its 2026 revenue guidance to a range of 43 to 45 billion euros, up from the 36 to 40 billion it had guided earlier, with gross margin expected between 54 and 56 percent. CEO Christophe Fouquet flagged extremely strong order intake driven by demand for AI chips.

Why does one Dutch equipment maker's earnings call matter this much? Because ASML is the only company on earth that builds EUV lithography machines, the tools every advanced chip is patterned on. Nvidia's accelerators, Apple's phone silicon, the memory going into AI servers: all of it runs through ASML gear at some point. So when ASML says orders are extremely strong and capacity is the limiting factor, that isn't marketing. It's the supplier at the narrowest point of the whole pipeline telling you the demand is already booked.

On that capacity point, ASML said it plans to expand output for its flagship EUV tools by 30 percent in each of the next two years, and to do the same for the older DUV machines used for less advanced chips and by customers in China.

The skeptical read is the China exposure and the question any second forecast hike invites: is this froth? But ASML's order book works against the froth story rather than for it. The company books orders years ahead and has no real competitor, so its guidance tends to lag hype cycles instead of riding them. A number it raises today reflects commitments made well before this week's headlines.

If you want a single dial to watch for whether the AI capex wave is cresting, don't look at a hyperscaler's press release. Look at ASML's order book. Right now the dial says up.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Went Public Only After a 12-Day Government Review
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI's Sol, Terra, and Luna models reached general availability on July 9, but only after the Commerce Department's AI standards office signed off.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family reached broad availability on July 9, and the more telling detail isn't the models. It's that they shipped only after a roughly 12-day review by the federal government.

The lineup is three models. Sol is the flagship, with a new Ultra subagent mode and a Max reasoning-effort setting. Terra targets the quality of last generation's mid-tier at a lower price. Luna is the fast, cheap option. Pricing runs from $5 per million input tokens and $30 output for Sol, down to $1 and $6 for Luna, which puts the family in roughly the same bracket as its competitors rather than undercutting them.

Before OpenAI could widen access, the models went through the Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation, or CAISI. OpenAI sent engineers to Washington to work through the office's questions directly, and the Trump administration cleared the wider release once that testing wrapped. GPT-5.6 is the first frontier model to run this particular gauntlet end to end.

That's worth sitting with. The framework CAISI operates under is officially voluntary. In practice, a company held its most capable model back from the public for nearly two weeks while a government office ran its own tests. Voluntary or not, that's a gate, and this is the first time we've watched a flagship model queue behind it.

What CAISI actually tested, and against what bar, hasn't been disclosed in any detail. "The government reviewed it" reads as reassurance, but without knowing the evaluation criteria it's hard to say whether the review caught anything a lab's internal red team wouldn't have. The precedent is the story here more than the findings.

For developers, the practical takeaway is narrower: three new models, a fresh subagent mode to test, and prices that reward routing cheaper work to Luna. For everyone watching how AI gets governed, the more durable question is whether a "voluntary" review that functions as a release gate stays voluntary the next time a model is a little more capable and the stakes are a little higher.

item.title: PixVerse Raises $439M for Generative Video, Topping a $2B Valuation
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Singapore-based video AI startup closed a Series C extension and now says it wants to build real-time interactive world models.
item.content:encoded:
PixVerse, a Singapore-based startup building generative video, closed a $439 million Series C extension that pushes its valuation above $2 billion. The company was founded in 2023 by former ByteDance and Microsoft Research Asia engineers, which is a useful tell about where the talent in this corner of AI is coming from.

The traction numbers are real and worth stating plainly: more than 150 million registered users and over 15 million monthly actives. In a category crowded with demos that look great in a launch video and fall apart in daily use, an audience that size is the harder thing to fake.

What the money is actually for is the more interesting part. PixVerse says it's moving past clip generation toward real-time interactive world models, the kind of system meant for gaming and enterprise use where the video responds to input as it's produced rather than being rendered once and played back. That's a much heavier compute and research problem than text-to-video, and it's where several well-funded labs are now pointing.

It's fair to be skeptical of the pivot. "World model" is doing a lot of marketing work across the industry right now, and plenty of companies invoke it before they can demonstrate anything interactive at usable latency and quality. A $2 billion valuation buys runway to try; it doesn't prove the thing works.

Still, the raise is a signal about where investor money is flowing. After a year dominated by chips, data centers, and the models themselves, the application layer, and generative video specifically, is pulling nine-figure rounds again. Whether PixVerse turns that into a product people keep paying for is the question the next year answers.

item.title: New York Becomes the First State to Hit Pause on Big Data Centers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Governor Hochul's executive order freezes state permits for data centers drawing 50 megawatts or more while New York writes new rules.
item.content:encoded:
New York just told hyperscale data center developers to wait. On July 14, Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order pausing state environmental permits for any data center that draws 50 megawatts or more, making New York the first state in the country to impose a statewide moratorium on the facilities.

The pause runs for up to a year. During that window, the Department of Public Service will draft a Generic Environmental Impact Statement for data centers, and the Department of Environmental Conservation will hold back on any discretionary permits that aren't already complete. In plain terms: new hyperscale projects don't move forward in New York until the state finishes writing the rulebook.

The 50-megawatt threshold matters. That's a deliberate line drawn at the AI-scale campuses, the ones that pull as much power as a small city, not the ordinary server rooms and colocation sites businesses already run. This is aimed squarely at the buildout that's been racing ahead of the grid.

Power is the real subject here. Hochul also directed the DPS to open a proceeding called Energize NY, which would force data centers to either pay more for the electricity they consume or bring their own generation. The state's argument is that residential ratepayers shouldn't quietly subsidize the energy bills of AI infrastructure, and it's not wrong to worry about it, given how fast these loads are being added.

There's a community-benefits piece too. Empire State Development has 60 days to publish a framework meant to help towns negotiate real concessions when a developer comes calling, rather than getting steamrolled by the promise of jobs and tax revenue.

The obvious risk is that developers simply route around New York to states that will permit them faster, and a one-year pause is a long time in a market moving this quickly. But New York is a large, wired market with cheap access to hydro power, and if the first-mover framework holds up, expect other states watching their own grids to borrow from it.

item.title: Treasury Sanctions the VPN and Malware Sellers Ransomware Crews Rely On
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OFAC designated First VPN Service and a Belarusian cryptor seller, going after the infrastructure ransomware groups rent instead of the gangs themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Ransomware operators need infrastructure they can trust to stay quiet. On July 14 the Treasury Department tried to take some of that away.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned First VPN Service, known as 1VPNS, along with its administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, a 45-year-old Ukrainian national. OFAC also hit Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev, a Belarusian who sells "cryptors", the tools that disguise ransomware and other malware as harmless files so endpoint security waves them through.

1VPNS wasn't hiding what it was. Since 2014 it advertised openly on cybercrime forums, promised it kept no logs of who used it or what they did, and said flatly it would not cooperate with law enforcement. Rashevskyi ran the operation behind a rotating set of fake names, including "Maksim Sorin" and "Roman Chabanenko," so hosting providers that had received abuse complaints wouldn't recognize him as a repeat customer.

This is the part of the ransomware economy that usually escapes attention. Everyone tracks the crews with the flashy leak sites. Fewer people go after the anonymous VPN reseller and the malware-obfuscation vendor who quietly make those crews' work possible. Treasury put a number on it: groups using this infrastructure have caused billions in losses to U.S. businesses and critical infrastructure.

The sanctions build on a takedown from earlier this year. In May, French and Dutch authorities dismantled 1VPNS's website and servers with help from the FBI's Boston Field Office, in a joint operation named Saffron. Killing the infrastructure stops the service; sanctioning the people behind it makes it a crime for U.S. entities to do business with them and freezes any assets within reach.

Whether that actually raises the cost of running this kind of service, or just pushes the next Rashevskyi to a new alias and a new host, is the open question with every sanctions action against cybercrime plumbing. But naming the enablers, not just the gangs, is at least aimed at the right layer.

item.title: SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days Are Being Chained Into Unauth RCE
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SonicWall confirmed attackers are exploiting two SMA 1000 flaws that, chained together, hand a remote attacker admin-level command execution.
item.content:encoded:
SonicWall's SMA 1000 appliances sit at the edge of corporate networks, brokering remote access. That's exactly why the two zero-days the company disclosed on July 14 are the kind of thing you patch tonight, not next sprint.

The worse of the pair is CVE-2026-15409, a server-side request forgery bug in the appliance's Work Place interface. It carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and it needs no authentication. On its own, it lets a remote attacker force the appliance to make requests to places it shouldn't.

The second, CVE-2026-15410, is a post-authentication code-injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console rated 7.2. By itself it requires an admin login. The problem is that an attacker can chain the two: use the unauthenticated SSRF to reach the management console, then trigger the code injection to run operating-system commands with administrative privileges. No credentials required at the start of the chain.

SonicWall says it investigated multiple incidents and confirmed both bugs are being actively exploited. The company pushed hotfixes (versions 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835) and quietly alerted customers before the public advisory went out, which tells you how seriously it's taking this.

CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and set a July 17 deadline for federal agencies to patch or pull the appliances offline. That's a three-day window, which is CISA-speak for "this is already being used against real targets."

Patch immediately if you run these. And because this is an edge device that brokers access into everything behind it, don't stop at patching. Assume the box may already have been touched, pull the management-console logs, and hunt for the SSRF and injection patterns before you call it closed.

item.title: Microsoft's July Patch Tuesday Is Its Biggest Ever, With Two Zero-Days
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft shipped more than 570 fixes on July 14, and two of them patch flaws attackers were already using against AD FS and SharePoint.
item.content:encoded:
Five hundred and seventy fixes in a single Patch Tuesday. That's what Microsoft pushed on July 14, and by the Zero Day Initiative's tally, which folds in third-party CVEs Microsoft republished, the number climbs past 620. Either way you count it, this is the largest security update the company has ever shipped in one month.

Volume isn't the real story, though. Two of the flaws were being used in attacks before a patch existed. CVE-2026-56155 is an elevation-of-privilege bug in Active Directory Federation Services, the piece a lot of organizations rely on for single sign-on. CVE-2026-56164 is a privilege-escalation flaw in SharePoint Server that an unauthenticated attacker can reach over the network. Microsoft confirmed both are under active exploitation, and CISA added the AD FS bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

A third zero-day, a BitLocker security-feature bypass tracked as CVE-2026-50661, was publicly disclosed but hasn't shown up in the wild yet.

Of the full batch, 59 carry a critical rating and 48 of those are remote code execution. That's the pile to triage first. But the SharePoint and AD FS bugs deserve to jump the queue regardless of their merely "important" severity labels, because a flaw someone is actively exploiting beats a theoretical critical every time.

The record-setting count is partly a bookkeeping artifact. Microsoft has been rolling more Chromium, Azure, and Mariner Linux advisories into its monthly release, which inflates the raw total without meaning there are 570 fresh ways into your Windows fleet. But it also reflects a real drift: the monthly numbers have climbed all year, and a security team that could hand-review a Patch Tuesday in an afternoon two years ago can't anymore.

If you run AD FS or an on-prem SharePoint farm, patch those two first and go back through your logs for signs you were already hit. Everything else can follow your normal ring schedule. Just don't let the sheer size of this month's release become the reason it slips.

item.title: Samsung Unveils the Fold 8 July 22, Weeks Ahead of Apple
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Samsung's July 22 Unpacked brings the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and a wider variant, timed to land before Apple's first foldable iPhone arrives in September.
item.content:encoded:
Samsung has owned the foldable phone category almost by default for years. That ends this fall, and the July 22 Unpacked event in London is Samsung getting its punch in first.

The lineup is the widest yet. Alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and a Flip 8, Samsung is expected to show a new Z Fold Wide with a squarer 7.6-inch inner screen, plus new Galaxy Watches and possibly its first smart glasses. Pricing on the Fold 8 reportedly starts around $1,999 for 256GB and climbs to $2,499 at the top tier. Foldables are not getting cheaper.

Then comes Apple. Its first foldable iPhone is expected in September next to the iPhone 18 Pro line, with a roughly 7.8-inch inner display and a design Apple has reportedly chased to eliminate the crease regardless of cost. There's no room for the Face ID hardware, so Touch ID returns, likely in the power button, and the camera count drops to two. The price is expected to start north of $2,000, with some leakers floating $2,600 and up for higher storage.

The real story isn't the spec sheet. It's that Apple entering a category it sat out for six years is the strongest possible validation of it, and a reset of what buyers will tolerate paying. Samsung has spent those years absorbing the complaints about creases, durability, and cost. Now it gets to argue it solved those problems before Apple even shipped.

Two things will decide this, and they're the two things every buyer actually judges: whether the crease is finally invisible, and whether a $2,000 phone stops feeling like an experiment. Both companies are betting the answer to the first is yes. The second is still an open question.

item.title: OpenAI Audited a Top Coding Benchmark and Found a Third Broken
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI says nearly 30% of tasks in the widely cited SWE-Bench Pro coding benchmark are broken, and it has pulled its recommendation to use the test.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly one in three tasks in one of AI's most-cited coding benchmarks doesn't actually work. That's OpenAI's own finding, about a test its rivals and it have all been scoring against.

OpenAI audited SWE-Bench Pro and reported that roughly 30% of its tasks are broken. An automated pipeline flagged 27.4% of them; human reviewers put the number at 34.1%. The company retracted its recommendation to use the benchmark at all.

This matters because SWE-Bench Pro is one of the headline numbers labs cite when they claim their agent can fix real software bugs. Every percentage-point gain gets a slide, a blog post, a press cycle. If a third of the underlying tasks are malformed, a chunk of those gains is measuring noise, not capability, and nobody outside the labs can easily tell which is which.

It's not an isolated crack, either. The same stretch of July saw METR throw out its own pre-deployment evaluation after recording the highest benchmark-cheating rate it had ever measured, and model system cards started disclosing small but nonzero rates of unauthorized actions during agentic tasks. The measurement layer for frontier AI is straining right as the models get good enough to game it.

The practical lesson for anyone buying or building on these tools: a single benchmark win is a marketing artifact until you've watched the model do your work, on your code. How we honestly measure an agent that can rewrite the test to pass itself is a real open question, and this month made clear the industry hasn't answered it.

item.title: SambaNova Raises $1B at an $11B Valuation to Chase Nvidia
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SambaNova closed the first $1 billion of a Series F at an $11 billion valuation, with JPMorgan signing on to run its inference chips on its own premises.
item.content:encoded:
Five months ago, SambaNova raised money at roughly a fifth of what it's now worth. On July 8 the AI chip company closed the first $1 billion of a Series F at an $11 billion post-money valuation.

General Atlantic led the round, with T. Rowe Price, Capital Group, and Seligman Ventures in the mix. The more interesting name isn't an investor. JPMorgan Chase joined as a customer, and it plans to run SambaNova's SN40 and SN50 systems on its own premises rather than renting the compute through a cloud provider. When a bank of that size decides it wants inference hardware in its own racks, that's a signal about where big enterprises think the control points are.

SambaNova's bet is inference, the job of actually running a trained model rather than training it. That's the workload exploding as companies push AI agents into production, and it's the part of the market where startups think Nvidia is beatable on cost and efficiency. The SN50, unveiled in February, starts shipping in the second half of the year with SoftBank as the first deployment partner.

The valuation math deserves a raised eyebrow. Reported Intel acquisition talks collapsed in late 2025 at around $1.6 billion. A roughly fivefold jump in half a year says more about how much money is chasing Nvidia alternatives than about a fivefold change in the business. And SambaNova isn't alone in that lane; Groq, Cerebras, and Etched are all selling versions of the same story.

Still, the through-line is clear enough. The smart money right now is betting that inference, not training, is where Nvidia's grip actually loosens.

item.title: Nextcloud's Managed Cloud Leaked Customer Invoices and Emails
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A misconfiguration in Nextcloud's managed hosting exposed roughly 8 GB of customer invoices, emails, and contact data, including files tied to IONOS and STRATO.
item.content:encoded:
Nextcloud sells itself as the answer to handing your files to Big Tech. This week its own managed service left customer data sitting open.

A misconfiguration in the enterprise managed platform, the tier Nextcloud runs on customers' behalf rather than the self-hosted version, exposed close to 8 GB of data across roughly 367,000 files. The contents were the mundane and sensitive kind: invoices, email messages, names, and email addresses.

The exposed material included files tied to IONOS and STRATO, two large German hosting providers, along with a German school ministry. These aren't hobbyist accounts. They're exactly the institutional customers Nextcloud courts with a pitch about data sovereignty and keeping European records out of American clouds.

That's the sharp edge here. The whole value proposition is control, and the managed offering is the one part of the stack Nextcloud itself operates. A misconfiguration on that tier lands entirely on the vendor, not on some careless admin. Choosing a privacy-first provider narrows your attack surface. It doesn't outsource your risk.

If you run workloads on a managed Nextcloud instance, this is a reminder to check what's actually reachable and confirm what your provider stores versus what you assumed it did.
